items.text: to get to the bottom of
items.meaning: To discover the real reason or cause of a problem.
items.example: We need to get to the bottom of why these errors are occurring before we can fix them.
items.plain: We need to understand the real cause of these errors before we can fix them.
items.note: Common in professional settings when investigating issues.

items.meaning: Used to clarify or explain the main point you are trying to make.
items.example: What I'm getting at is, we need a more robust system to prevent this from happening again.
items.plain: My main point is that we need a more robust system to prevent this from happening again.
items.note: Helps to rephrase or emphasize a point, often when the listener seems confused.

items.meaning: To mention an issue or worry that you have about something.
items.example: I wanted to raise a concern about the timeline for the project; it seems quite ambitious.
items.plain: I wanted to mention my worry about the project timeline; it seems quite ambitious.
items.note: A polite and professional way to introduce a potential problem.

items.meaning: To carefully consider all available choices before making a decision.
items.example: Before we decide, let's take some time to weigh the options and their potential impact.
items.plain: Before we decide, let's take some time to consider all the choices and their potential impact.
items.note: Implies a thoughtful and analytical approach to decision-making.

items.text: to come up with a solution
items.meaning: To think of or create an answer to a problem.
items.example: We need to brainstorm quickly and come up with a solution for the unexpected budget cut.
items.plain: We need to brainstorm quickly and find an answer for the unexpected budget cut.
items.note: Focuses on the act of generating a resolution.

items.text: to be on the same page
items.meaning: To have a shared understanding or agreement about a situation or plan.
items.example: Let's quickly review the action points to ensure we're all on the same page.
items.plain: Let's quickly review the action points to ensure we all understand and agree.
items.note: Essential for team collaboration and avoiding misunderstandings.

items.meaning: To resolve small problems or disagreements in a plan or agreement.
items.example: We've agreed on the main strategy, now we just need to iron out the details of implementation.
items.plain: We've agreed on the main strategy, now we just need to resolve the small problems of implementation.
items.note: Suggests a process of refining and perfecting a plan.

items.meaning: To approach a situation in a practical and realistic way, focusing on what works.
items.example: Given the limited resources, we need to take a pragmatic view of what's achievable.
items.plain: Given the limited resources, we need to be practical and realistic about what's achievable.
items.note: Emphasizes practicality over idealism, common in business discussions.

items.meaning: To gain agreement and support from others for a plan or idea.
items.example: We won't be able to proceed until we get buy-in from all the key stakeholders.
items.plain: We won't be able to proceed until we gain agreement and support from all the key stakeholders.
items.note: Crucial for successful project implementation, especially in larger organizations.

items.meaning: To briefly communicate with someone, often to check in or update.
items.example: Let's touch base again on Friday to see how the new process is working out.
items.plain: Let's communicate briefly again on Friday to see how the new process is working out.
items.note: Informal yet professional, used for quick check-ins.

items.meaning: To return to a previous topic or issue later.
items.example: That's a good point, but let's circle back to it after we've discussed the main agenda items.
items.plain: That's a good point, but let's return to it after we've discussed the main agenda items.
items.note: Useful for managing meeting agendas and deferring discussions politely.

items.meaning: To monitor or watch something carefully.
items.example: I'll keep an eye on the budget projections to ensure we don't overspend this quarter.
items.plain: I'll monitor the budget projections to ensure we don't overspend this quarter.
items.note: Implies ongoing vigilance and responsibility.

items.meaning: To deal with a problem or concern directly and effectively.
items.example: We need to address the issue of low team morale before it impacts productivity further.
items.plain: We need to deal with the problem of low team morale before it impacts productivity further.
items.note: A direct and professional way to state the need for action.

items.text: to put a plan in place
items.meaning: To establish a detailed strategy or set of actions.
items.example: Once we've identified the root cause, we can put a plan in place to prevent recurrence.
items.plain: Once we've identified the root cause, we can establish a strategy to prevent recurrence.
items.note: Emphasizes the formal creation and implementation of a strategy.

items.meaning: To describe the subsequent actions that need to be taken.
items.example: Before we adjourn, let's quickly outline the next steps and assign responsibilities.
items.plain: Before we adjourn, let's quickly describe the subsequent actions and assign responsibilities.
items.note: Provides clarity and structure for moving forward after a discussion.

items.text: to get to the crux of
items.meaning: To identify the most important or fundamental part of a problem or matter.
items.example: We spent too long on minor points; let's try to get to the crux of the matter.
items.plain: We spent too long on minor points; let's try to identify the most important part of the matter.
items.note: Suggests a desire to focus on the core issue, often after tangential discussions.

items.meaning: To temporarily disengage from a situation to gain a broader perspective.
items.example: This problem is complex; perhaps we should take a step back and look at it from a different angle.
items.plain: This problem is complex; perhaps we should temporarily disengage and look at it from a different angle.
items.note: Useful when feeling overwhelmed or stuck, encouraging a fresh perspective.

items.meaning: To achieve a better understanding of a situation or problem.
items.example: I'd like to speak with Sarah to gain some clarity on her team's current workload.
items.plain: I'd like to speak with Sarah to better understand her team's current workload.
items.note: Implies seeking specific information to resolve ambiguity.

items.meaning: To understand and be able to manage a situation or problem.
items.example: It took a few weeks, but I think I'm finally starting to get a handle on the new software.
items.plain: It took a few weeks, but I think I'm finally starting to understand and manage the new software.
items.note: Suggests gaining control and competence over something challenging.

items.meaning: To act in anticipation of future problems, needs, or changes.
items.example: We need to be proactive in identifying potential risks, rather than just reacting to them.
items.plain: We need to act in anticipation of potential risks, rather than just reacting to them.
items.note: Emphasizes foresight and taking initiative.

items.meaning: To deal with a situation carefully and thoughtfully, avoiding hasty actions.
items.example: This is a sensitive issue, so we should take a measured approach to our response.
items.plain: This is a sensitive issue, so we should deal with our response carefully and thoughtfully.
items.note: Suggests prudence and a well-considered strategy.

items.text: to err on the side of caution
items.form: err on the side of caution
items.meaning: To choose the safer or less risky option, even if it means being overly careful.
items.example: I think we should err on the side of caution and double-check all the figures before submitting.
items.plain: I think we should choose the safer option and double-check all the figures before submitting.
items.note: A common idiom for recommending a conservative approach.

items.meaning: To be in a difficult situation requiring a choice between two undesirable options.
items.example: We face a dilemma: either delay the launch or release with known bugs.
items.plain: We are in a difficult situation: either delay the launch or release with known bugs.
items.note: Highlights a challenging choice with no easy answer.

items.meaning: To be in a difficult or awkward situation.
items.example: If we lose that client, we'll really be in a bind financially for the next quarter.
items.plain: If we lose that client, we'll really be in a difficult situation financially for the next quarter.
items.note: Informal but widely used in professional contexts to describe a predicament.

items.meaning: To be facing significant difficulties or strong opposition.
items.example: With the tight deadline and limited staff, we're really up against it to finish on time.
items.plain: With the tight deadline and limited staff, we're really facing significant difficulties to finish on time.
items.note: Conveys a sense of struggle against challenging circumstances.

items.meaning: To have too much work or too many responsibilities, leading to being overworked.
items.example: Everyone on the team is stretched thin, so adding another project right now isn't feasible.
items.plain: Everyone on the team has too much work, so adding another project right now isn't feasible.
items.note: A common way to describe resource constraints and workload issues.

items.meaning: To be at a point where an important decision must be made, with significant consequences.
items.example: The company is at a crossroads, needing to decide whether to expand internationally or focus domestically.
items.plain: The company is at a point where an important decision must be made, needing to decide whether to expand internationally or focus domestically.
items.note: Implies a critical juncture requiring careful consideration.

items.meaning: To be in a new or unfamiliar situation with no previous experience to guide you.
items.example: Implementing this new technology means we're in uncharted territory, so we'll learn as we go.
items.plain: Implementing this new technology means we're in a new situation, so we'll learn as we go.
items.note: Highlights novelty and the need for adaptability.

items.meaning: To be in a precarious or risky situation, where one wrong move could lead to trouble.
items.example: After missing two deadlines, John is really on thin ice with the project manager.
items.plain: After missing two deadlines, John is in a precarious situation with the project manager.
items.note: Implies a warning or a delicate situation requiring extreme care.

items.meaning: To be subjected to close and careful examination or observation.
items.example: Our department is currently under scrutiny due to the recent performance dip.
items.plain: Our department is currently being closely examined due to the recent performance dip.
items.note: Suggests a period of intense review, often implying potential problems.

items.meaning: To be in the process of being formally examined or evaluated.
items.example: The new proposal is currently under review by the executive committee.
items.plain: The new proposal is currently being formally examined by the executive committee.
items.note: A neutral term for an ongoing evaluation process.

items.meaning: To be the subject of conversation or debate.
items.example: The possibility of extending the project deadline is still under discussion.
items.plain: The possibility of extending the project deadline is still being talked about.
items.note: Indicates that a topic is being actively considered but not yet decided.

items.meaning: To fully understand the reality of a difficult situation, without false hopes.
items.example: I'm under no illusion that this will be an easy task; it will require significant effort.
items.plain: I fully understand that this will not be an easy task; it will require significant effort.
items.note: Expresses a realistic and often sober assessment of a challenge.

items.meaning: To believe something, often based on indirect information, which may or may not be true.
items.example: I was under the impression that the report was due next Friday, not this Friday.
items.plain: I believed that the report was due next Friday, not this Friday.
items.note: Used to politely correct a misunderstanding or state a belief that might be wrong.

items.meaning: To consider a situation in relation to other facts, to understand its true importance.
items.example: Let's put things in perspective; while this setback is frustrating, it's not a catastrophic failure.
items.plain: Let's consider other facts; while this setback is frustrating, it's not a catastrophic failure.
items.note: Helps to calm anxieties and provide a balanced view of a problem.

items.meaning: To resolve misunderstandings or bad feelings between people.
items.example: There's been some tension, so I think we need to meet to clear the air about the project roles.
items.plain: There's been some tension, so I think we need to meet to resolve misunderstandings about the project roles.
items.note: Focuses on improving interpersonal relations after conflict.

items.meaning: To connect two things or groups that are separate or different.
items.example: We need to find a way to bridge the gap between the sales and marketing teams' objectives.
items.plain: We need to find a way to connect the sales and marketing teams' different objectives.
items.note: Implies resolving differences or creating synergy.

items.meaning: To discover shared interests, beliefs, or areas of agreement.
items.example: Despite our initial disagreements, I'm confident we can find common ground on the budget.
items.plain: Despite our initial disagreements, I'm confident we can discover shared interests on the budget.
items.note: Essential for negotiation and reaching consensus.

items.meaning: To ensure that others have realistic ideas about what is possible or likely.
items.example: We need to manage expectations with the client about how quickly we can deliver the new features.
items.plain: We need to ensure the client has realistic ideas about how quickly we can deliver the new features.
items.note: Prevents disappointment by setting realistic boundaries.

items.meaning: To make a potential problem or danger less severe or serious.
items.example: We've implemented new security protocols to mitigate the risk of data breaches.
items.plain: We've implemented new security protocols to make the risk of data breaches less severe.
items.note: A key term in project management and strategic planning.

items.meaning: To accept responsibility for something, especially a problem or task.
items.example: Someone needs to take ownership of this bug and ensure it gets fixed promptly.
items.plain: Someone needs to accept responsibility for this bug and ensure it gets fixed promptly.
items.note: Emphasizes accountability and initiative.

items.meaning: To gain knowledge or improve behavior by reflecting on past errors.
items.example: This project didn't go as planned, but we must learn from our mistakes for next time.
items.plain: This project didn't go as planned, but we must gain knowledge from our past errors for next time.
items.note: A common phrase for promoting growth and continuous improvement.

items.meaning: To overcome a problem or difficult situation and continue forward.
items.example: We've spent enough time dwelling on what went wrong; it's time to move past this.
items.plain: We've spent enough time dwelling on what went wrong; it's time to overcome this.
items.note: Encourages forward momentum and resolution.

items.text: to keep lines of communication open
items.meaning: To ensure that people continue to talk to each other and share information.
items.example: It's vital to keep lines of communication open between departments during this transition.
items.plain: It's vital to ensure people continue to talk to each other between departments during this transition.
items.note: Stresses the importance of ongoing dialogue to prevent issues.

items.meaning: To make certain that individuals or teams are responsible for their actions and outcomes.
items.example: We need clearer roles to ensure accountability for each stage of the project.
items.plain: We need clearer roles to make certain that individuals are responsible for each stage of the project.
items.note: A formal term for establishing responsibility.

items.text: to get things back on track
items.meaning: To restore a project or situation to its normal or desired course after a deviation.
items.example: The delay was significant, but we're working hard to get things back on track.
items.plain: The delay was significant, but we're working hard to restore the situation to its desired course.
items.note: Implies corrective action to return to a planned schedule or state.

items.meaning: To confront a problem directly and without avoidance.
items.example: This conflict won't resolve itself; we need to address the issue head-on.
items.plain: This conflict won't resolve itself; we need to confront the problem directly.
items.note: Suggests courage and a direct approach to difficult problems.

items.meaning: To cause something to cease or end.
items.example: We need to put a stop to these recurring errors by implementing stricter quality checks.
items.plain: We need to cause these recurring errors to end by implementing stricter quality checks.
items.note: Implies decisive action to terminate an undesirable situation.

items.text: to get ahead of the curve
items.meaning: To be in front of current trends or developments, anticipating future needs.
items.example: By investing in new technology now, we can get ahead of the curve in market innovation.
items.plain: By investing in new technology now, we can be in front of current trends in market innovation.
items.note: Focuses on proactive strategy and competitive advantage.

items.meaning: To adopt an attitude or position of acting in anticipation of future problems or needs.
items.example: Instead of waiting for problems, we should take a proactive stance on risk management.
items.plain: Instead of waiting for problems, we should adopt an attitude of acting in anticipation of risk.
items.note: Similar to "to be proactive" but emphasizes the deliberate adoption of this approach.

items.meaning: To be careful and prudent in one's actions or decisions.
items.example: We should exercise caution when dealing with this new vendor until we build trust.
items.plain: We should be careful when dealing with this new vendor until we build trust.
items.note: A formal way to advise prudence.

items.text: to be in a tight spot
items.meaning: To be in a difficult or awkward situation.
items.example: If we don't secure that funding, we'll be in a tight spot regarding project completion.
items.plain: If we don't secure that funding, we'll be in a difficult situation regarding project completion.
items.note: Similar to "in a bind," but perhaps slightly more common in general conversation.

items.text: to be caught in the crossfire
items.meaning: To be unintentionally involved in a conflict between other people or groups.
items.example: I feel like I'm caught in the crossfire between the two department heads arguing over resources.
items.plain: I feel like I'm unintentionally involved in the conflict between the two department heads arguing over resources.
items.note: Describes being an innocent party affected by others' disputes.

items.text: to be in the firing line
items.meaning: To be in a position where one is likely to be criticized or blamed.
items.example: If this project fails, the whole team will be in the firing line, not just the manager.
items.plain: If this project fails, the whole team will be in a position to be criticized, not just the manager.
items.note: Suggests vulnerability to criticism or negative consequences.

items.meaning: To be subjected to extremely close and detailed examination.
items.example: After the audit, our financial records are really under the microscope.
items.plain: After the audit, our financial records are being extremely closely examined.
items.note: Stronger than "under scrutiny," implying intense and detailed inspection.

items.meaning: To be being thought about or discussed.
items.example: Your proposal for the new marketing campaign is currently under consideration.
items.plain: Your proposal for the new marketing campaign is currently being thought about.
items.note: A formal way to indicate that something is being evaluated.

items.meaning: To be in the process of being discussed in order to reach an agreement.
items.example: The terms of the new contract are still under negotiation with the supplier.
items.plain: The terms of the new contract are still being discussed to reach an agreement with the supplier.
items.note: Indicates an ongoing process of bargaining and discussion.

items.meaning: To be kept secret or hidden from public knowledge.
items.example: The details of the new product launch are still under wraps until the official announcement.
items.plain: The details of the new product launch are still being kept secret until the official announcement.
items.note: Used for confidential information or plans.

items.meaning: To be in progress; happening now.
items.example: The implementation of the new system is now under way and progressing well.
items.plain: The implementation of the new system is now in progress and progressing well.
items.note: A formal way to state that an activity has started and is continuing.

items.meaning: To maintain the speed or progress of an activity.
items.example: We've had a great start to the project; let's keep momentum going with regular updates.
items.plain: We've had a great start to the project; let's maintain the progress with regular updates.
items.note: Focuses on sustaining positive progress and energy.

items.meaning: To make a choice based on a thorough understanding of the facts and options.
items.example: We need more data before we can make an informed decision about the investment.
items.plain: We need more data before we can make a choice based on a thorough understanding about the investment.
items.note: Emphasizes the importance of data and knowledge in decision-making.

items.meaning: To arrive at a general agreement among a group of people.
items.example: It's important that we discuss this until we can reach a consensus on the best path forward.
items.plain: It's important that we discuss this until we can arrive at a general agreement on the best path forward.
items.note: Highlights the goal of collective agreement, often after discussion.

items.meaning: To present an idea or plan for consideration.
items.example: I'd like to put forward a proposal for restructuring the customer support team.
items.plain: I'd like to present an idea for restructuring the customer support team.
items.note: A formal way to introduce a suggestion or plan.

items.meaning: To suggest an idea tentatively to see how others react to it.
items.example: I just wanted to float an idea about a new marketing campaign; it's still very rough.
items.plain: I just wanted to suggest an idea tentatively about a new marketing campaign; it's still very rough.
items.note: Implies a preliminary suggestion, inviting feedback.

items.meaning: To investigate other possible options or solutions.
items.example: If this approach doesn't work, we'll need to explore alternatives quickly.
items.plain: If this approach doesn't work, we'll need to investigate other possible options quickly.
items.note: Suggests a willingness to consider different paths if the current one fails.

items.meaning: To propose an idea or plan for someone to consider.
items.example: May I offer a suggestion on how we might streamline this particular process?
items.plain: May I propose an idea on how we might streamline this particular process?
items.note: A polite and formal way to contribute an idea.

items.meaning: To be a practical and achievable course of action.
items.example: Outsourcing this task could be a viable path if we can't hire more staff internally.
items.plain: Outsourcing this task could be a practical and achievable course of action if we can't hire more staff internally.
items.note: Assesses the feasibility and effectiveness of an option.

items.meaning: To regularly check the development or improvement of something.
items.example: We need to monitor progress closely on the new software rollout to catch any issues early.
items.plain: We need to regularly check the development closely on the new software rollout to catch any issues early.
items.note: Essential for project management and ensuring goals are met.

items.meaning: To formally examine and assess the current state of affairs.
items.example: Let's schedule a meeting next week to review the situation after the initial implementation phase.
items.plain: Let's schedule a meeting next week to formally examine the current state of affairs after the initial implementation phase.
items.note: Implies a formal assessment or evaluation.

items.meaning: To make certain that a plan or system is put into effect without problems.
items.example: We need a detailed checklist to ensure smooth implementation of the new policy.
items.plain: We need a detailed checklist to make certain that the new policy is put into effect without problems.
items.note: Focuses on the execution phase of a plan.

items.meaning: To arrange a subsequent meeting or communication to check on progress or discuss further.
items.example: Let's schedule a follow-up for next month to discuss the long-term impact of these changes.
items.plain: Let's arrange a subsequent meeting for next month to discuss the long-term impact of these changes.
items.note: A standard professional practice for ongoing management.

items.meaning: To ensure that everyone involved has the same goals and understanding.
items.example: Before we start, let's quickly discuss the objectives to make sure we're aligned.
items.plain: Before we start, let's quickly discuss the objectives to ensure everyone has the same goals and understanding.
items.note: Crucial for team cohesion and preventing conflicting efforts.

items.meaning: A request for current information on the progress of a task or project.
items.example: Before the meeting, could you send out a quick email with what's the status update on your tasks?
items.plain: Before the meeting, could you send out a quick email with current information on the progress of your tasks?
items.note: A common and direct way to ask for progress reports.

items.meaning: To make small adjustments to improve something.
items.example: The new process is working well, but we still need to fine-tune a few steps for efficiency.
items.plain: The new process is working well, but we still need to make small adjustments to a few steps for efficiency.
items.note: Implies making minor, precise improvements.

items.meaning: To recognize and show that you understand someone's worry or issue.
items.example: I want to acknowledge a concern raised by the team about the increased workload.
items.plain: I want to recognize and show that I understand the worry raised by the team about the increased workload.
items.note: A diplomatic way to show empathy and validate another's point.

items.meaning: To accept the duty of dealing with something or being accountable for it.
items.example: I will take responsibility for coordinating the next phase of the project.
items.plain: I will accept the duty of coordinating the next phase of the project.
items.note: A formal way to state one's commitment to a task or outcome.

items.meaning: To experience a minor, temporary problem or delay.
items.example: We might have a slight hiccup with the server migration, but it should be resolved quickly.
items.plain: We might experience a minor, temporary problem with the server migration, but it should be resolved quickly.
items.note: An understated way to refer to a small, usually manageable issue.

items.meaning: To observe a recurring trend or sequence of events.
items.example: I've noticed a pattern emerging in the customer feedback, suggesting a common usability issue.
items.plain: I've observed a recurring trend in the customer feedback, suggesting a common usability issue.
items.note: Used when identifying a trend that might indicate a systemic problem.

items.text: there's a bit of a disconnect
items.form: there's a bit of a disconnect
items.meaning: There is a lack of connection or understanding between two things or people.
items.example: It seems there's a bit of a disconnect between what the client expects and what we can deliver.
items.plain: It seems there's a lack of connection between what the client expects and what we can deliver.
items.note: A polite way to point out a gap in understanding or alignment.

items.meaning: To discuss or consider something again, often because new information has emerged.
items.example: Given the new budget constraints, we might need to revisit this decision about the software upgrade.
items.plain: Given the new budget constraints, we might need to discuss this decision about the software upgrade again.
items.note: Suggests a need to re-evaluate a previous choice or plan.

items.meaning: A polite and understated way to express worry or apprehension.
items.example: I'm a little concerned about the potential impact of these changes on team morale.
items.plain: I'm worried about the potential impact of these changes on team morale.
items.note: A soft opening for expressing a reservation, often to invite discussion.

items.text: it's come to my attention that
items.form: It's come to my attention that
items.meaning: A formal way to introduce information you have recently learned, often about a problem.
items.example: It's come to my attention that some deadlines are being consistently missed.
items.plain: I've recently learned that some deadlines are being consistently missed.
items.note: Formal and often used when addressing an issue that needs to be resolved.

items.meaning: To encounter an unexpected difficulty or obstacle.
items.example: We've run into a snag with the data migration, which might delay the launch.
items.plain: We've encountered an unexpected difficulty with the data migration, which might delay the launch.
items.note: Informal but common, referring to a minor but disruptive problem.

items.meaning: A question asking for the fundamental underlying reason for a problem.
items.example: Before we implement any fixes, we need to understand what's the root cause of these system failures.
items.plain: Before we implement any fixes, we need to understand the fundamental reason for these system failures.
items.note: Focuses on deep analysis rather than superficial solutions.

items.meaning: To analyze or discuss a complex issue in more detail.
items.example: This feedback is quite broad; let's unpack this a bit to identify specific actionable points.
items.plain: This feedback is quite broad; let's analyze this in more detail to identify specific actionable points.
items.note: Suggests a collaborative and detailed examination of a topic.

items.meaning: To confront a difficult situation or task.
items.example: Our team will face a challenge in integrating the new software with our legacy systems.
items.plain: Our team will confront a difficult situation in integrating the new software with our legacy systems.
items.note: A neutral and professional way to describe a difficulty.

items.meaning: To examine something in more detail or to a deeper level.
items.example: The initial report shows an issue, but we need to drill down into the data to understand why.
items.plain: The initial report shows an issue, but we need to examine the data in more detail to understand why.
items.note: Common in data analysis and problem-solving discussions.

items.meaning: I am noticing a warning sign that indicates a potential problem or danger.
items.example: I'm seeing a red flag with the supplier's inconsistent delivery times; we should investigate.
items.plain: I am noticing a warning sign with the supplier's inconsistent delivery times; we should investigate.
items.note: Used to alert others to a potential issue that requires attention.

items.meaning: This has the potential to cause difficulties or issues.
items.example: If we don't secure the necessary permits, this could be problematic for the construction schedule.
items.plain: If we don't secure the necessary permits, this has the potential to cause difficulties for the construction schedule.
items.note: A polite and slightly understated way to express concern about a potential issue.

items.meaning: Something doesn't seem logical or consistent, suggesting a discrepancy.
items.example: The numbers in the report are conflicting; it's not quite adding up.
items.plain: The numbers in the report are conflicting; it doesn't seem logical.
items.note: Used when something feels wrong or inconsistent, prompting further investigation.

items.meaning: A minor difficulty that makes a situation more complex.
items.example: There's a slight complication with the scheduling, but I think we can work around it.
items.plain: There's a minor difficulty with the scheduling, but I think we can work around it.
items.note: An understated way to refer to a small, manageable problem.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a possible course of action or solution.
items.example: One option would be to reallocate resources from a less critical project.
items.plain: A possible course of action would be to reallocate resources from a less critical project.
items.note: A common and polite way to suggest a solution.

items.meaning: Used to propose an idea or approach for consideration.
items.example: What if we tried a different vendor for the raw materials to cut costs?
items.plain: How about we try a different vendor for the raw materials to cut costs?
items.note: An open-ended question inviting collaborative brainstorming.

items.text: we could explore the possibility of
items.form: We could explore the possibility of
items.meaning: Used to suggest investigating a potential course of action.
items.example: We could explore the possibility of extending the deadline if the team needs more time.
items.plain: We could investigate the potential course of action of extending the deadline if the team needs more time.
items.note: A diplomatic and collaborative way to suggest a new avenue.

items.meaning: A polite and tentative way to suggest a course of action or idea.
items.example: Perhaps we should consider the long-term implications before making a hasty decision.
items.plain: Maybe we should think about the long-term implications before making a hasty decision.
items.note: Softens a suggestion, making it less direct and more open to discussion.

items.meaning: Used to share a first idea or preliminary plan.
items.example: My initial thought is to prioritize the critical bugs and then address the minor ones.
items.plain: My first idea is to prioritize the critical bugs and then address the minor ones.
items.note: Indicates a starting point for discussion, not a final decision.

items.meaning: To argue against an idea or plan, not because you disagree, but to test its strength.
items.example: Just to play devil's advocate, what if the new system fails completely?
items.plain: Just to test the idea, what if the new system fails completely?
items.note: Used to introduce a challenging perspective for robust discussion.

items.meaning: To try a different method or approach to a problem.
items.example: Our current strategy isn't working; we need to take a different tack to solve this.
items.plain: Our current strategy isn't working; we need to try a different method to solve this.
items.note: Suggests a change in strategy or direction.

items.meaning: To implement a plan in stages rather than all at once.
items.example: Given the complexity, we should try a phased approach to the software rollout.
items.plain: Given the complexity, we should implement the software rollout in stages.
items.note: A common strategy for managing large or complex projects.

items.meaning: To generate a large number of creative ideas quickly, often in a group.
items.example: Let's take 15 minutes to brainstorm some ideas for improving team collaboration.
items.plain: Let's take 15 minutes to generate a large number of ideas for improving team collaboration.
items.note: Focuses on creative, uninhibited idea generation.

items.meaning: A question asking for the available choices or courses of action.
items.example: The client rejected our proposal, so what are our options here?
items.plain: The client rejected our proposal, so what are our available choices?
items.note: A direct question to initiate discussion about possible solutions.

items.meaning: To think about a situation or problem from every possible perspective.
items.example: Before we make a final decision, let's consider all angles of this complex issue.
items.plain: Before we make a final decision, let's think about every possible perspective of this complex issue.
items.note: Emphasizes thoroughness and comprehensive analysis.

items.meaning: The main or essential point of a complex situation or discussion.
items.example: Ultimately, it boils down to whether we have the resources to execute this plan.
items.plain: Ultimately, the main point is whether we have the resources to execute this plan.
items.note: Used to summarize or simplify a complex matter to its core essence.

items.meaning: The most important element that influences a choice or outcome.
items.example: The deciding factor is often the cost, even if other options seem better.
items.plain: The most important element is often the cost, even if other options seem better.
items.note: Highlights the critical element that determines a decision.

items.meaning: Let's make a decision.
items.example: We've discussed this enough; let's make a call on the best way forward.
items.plain: We've discussed this enough; let's make a decision on the best way forward.
items.note: Informal but common, used to prompt a decision after discussion.

items.text: to commit to a course of action
items.form: commit to a course of action
items.meaning: To firmly decide on a particular plan or strategy.
items.example: Once we commit to a course of action, we need to stick to it.
items.plain: Once we firmly decide on a particular plan, we need to stick to it.
items.note: Emphasizes firm decision-making and follow-through.

items.text: this seems like the most sensible approach
items.form: this seems like the most sensible approach
items.meaning: This appears to be the most reasonable and practical way to deal with something.
items.example: Given our current constraints, this seems like the most sensible approach.
items.plain: Given our current constraints, this appears to be the most reasonable and practical way.
items.note: A polite way to express a preference for a particular solution.

items.meaning: I am tending to favor a particular option or decision.
items.example: I'm leaning towards the option that offers long-term sustainability, despite higher initial costs.
items.plain: I am tending to favor the option that offers long-term sustainability, despite higher initial costs.
items.note: Expresses a preference without being definitive, inviting further discussion.

items.text: to give it the green light
items.meaning: To give official permission for something to proceed.
items.example: Once legal reviews it, we can give it the green light to start production.
items.plain: Once legal reviews it, we can give official permission to start production.
items.note: Informal but widely understood, meaning approval to proceed.

items.meaning: To determine the order of importance for tasks or issues.
items.example: We have too many tasks; we need to prioritize what's most critical for this week.
items.plain: We have too many tasks; we need to determine the order of importance for what's most critical for this week.
items.note: A fundamental action in problem-solving and project management.

items.meaning: It is a difficult decision to make.
items.example: Choosing between these two excellent candidates, it's a tough call.
items.plain: Choosing between these two excellent candidates, it is a difficult decision to make.
items.note: Informal but common, acknowledging the difficulty of a choice.

items.meaning: The best or most favorable answer to a problem.
items.example: Finding the optimal solution for resource allocation will save us significant time.
items.plain: Finding the best answer for resource allocation will save us significant time.
items.note: A formal term for the most effective or efficient resolution.

items.meaning: To carefully consider all available choices before making a decision.
items.example: Let's take a moment to weigh up the options before we vote on the proposal.
items.plain: Let's take a moment to carefully consider all available choices before we vote on the proposal.
items.note: Similar to "weigh the options," common in British English.

items.meaning: Let's proceed with this plan or decision.
items.example: We've discussed it thoroughly, so let's move forward with this approach.
items.plain: We've discussed it thoroughly, so let's proceed with this approach.
items.note: Used to signal the end of discussion and the start of action.

items.meaning: To reach a final decision or judgment after consideration.
items.example: After reviewing all the data, we've come to a conclusion about the best strategy.
items.plain: After reviewing all the data, we've reached a final decision about the best strategy.
items.note: Implies a definitive outcome after a process of analysis.

items.text: this feels like the right direction
items.form: this feels like the right direction
items.meaning: This seems to be the correct or most appropriate course of action.
items.example: Based on the feedback, this feels like the right direction for the project.
items.plain: Based on the feedback, this seems to be the correct course of action for the project.
items.note: Expresses a strong intuition or general agreement about a path.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a personal opinion or observation, often with a degree of politeness or tentativeness.
items.example: It seems to me that we're overlooking a simpler solution to this scheduling conflict.
items.plain: I think we're overlooking a simpler solution to this scheduling conflict.
items.note: A polite and common way to offer an opinion, suggesting it's a personal view rather than a definitive statement.

items.meaning: Used to state a specific worry or apprehension about a situation or proposed action.
items.example: My concern is that the new timeline might not be realistic given our current resources.
items.plain: I'm worried that the new timeline might not be realistic given our current resources.
items.note: Directly expresses a worry in a professional and clear manner, inviting discussion.

items.meaning: Used to highlight a specific anxiety or aspect of a situation that causes apprehension.
items.example: What worries me is the potential for this issue to escalate if we don't act quickly.
items.plain: I'm anxious about the potential for this issue to escalate if we don't act quickly.
items.note: Emphasizes the specific element causing concern, often used when a problem is developing.

items.meaning: Used to identify and articulate the main difficulty or obstacle in a situation.
items.example: The challenge here is balancing the client's demands with our team's capacity.
items.plain: The main difficulty is balancing the client's demands with our team's capacity.
items.note: Clearly defines the core problem, framing it as something to be overcome.

items.meaning: Used to summarize the most important point or conclusion from a discussion or analysis.
items.example: The key takeaway is that we need to improve internal communication to avoid future misunderstandings.
items.plain: The most important point is that we need to improve internal communication to avoid future misunderstandings.
items.note: Common in business and academic contexts to highlight the main learning or conclusion.

items.meaning: Used to highlight an important piece of information that should be considered.
items.example: It's worth noting that similar problems arose during the last project launch.
items.plain: We should remember that similar problems arose during the last project launch.
items.note: A polite way to draw attention to a relevant fact without being overly assertive.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize a crucial fact or principle that should not be forgotten.
items.example: It's important to remember that our primary goal is customer satisfaction, even with this setback.
items.plain: We must not forget that our primary goal is customer satisfaction, even with this setback.
items.note: A strong reminder of a fundamental point, often used to refocus a discussion.

items.meaning: Used to state a requirement or a necessary condition for success.
items.example: We need to ensure that all team members understand their roles in the new process.
items.plain: We must make sure that all team members understand their roles in the new process.
items.note: Highlights a critical action or outcome that must be guaranteed.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize the urgency or extreme importance of a particular action.
items.example: It's crucial that we address these security vulnerabilities before the next update.
items.plain: It's extremely important that we address these security vulnerabilities before the next update.
items.note: Conveys a strong sense of necessity and high stakes, often used in serious situations.

items.meaning: Used to express a tentative opinion or a leaning towards a particular belief.
items.example: I'm inclined to think that a phased rollout would minimize potential disruptions.
items.plain: I tend to believe that a phased rollout would minimize potential disruptions.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal way to offer an opinion, suggesting it's a considered view.

items.meaning: Used to state a formal or considered opinion, often in a professional context.
items.example: I'm of the opinion that we should prioritize long-term stability over short-term gains.
items.plain: I believe that we should prioritize long-term stability over short-term gains.
items.note: More formal than 'I think', suitable for serious discussions or when stating a firm stance.

items.meaning: Used to express doubt or skepticism about a statement, argument, or plan.
items.example: I'm not convinced that simply adding more staff will solve the underlying efficiency problem.
items.plain: I don't believe that simply adding more staff will solve the underlying efficiency problem.
items.note: Politely expresses disagreement or a need for more evidence, without being confrontational.

items.meaning: Used to express slight disapproval or unease about a situation or proposal.
items.example: I'm not entirely comfortable with the idea of proceeding without a clear risk assessment.
items.plain: I feel uneasy about the idea of proceeding without a clear risk assessment.
items.note: A diplomatic way to voice reservations or concerns, suggesting a need for caution.

items.meaning: Used to express skepticism or a lack of full belief in an idea or proposal.
items.example: I'm not entirely sold on the new marketing strategy; I think it needs more refinement.
items.plain: I'm not fully convinced by the new marketing strategy; I think it needs more refinement.
items.note: Informal but common in professional settings to express reservations about an idea.

items.meaning: Used to express a lack of full understanding about a specific detail or aspect.
items.example: I'm not entirely clear on the exact responsibilities of each team member in this new structure.
items.plain: I don't fully understand the exact responsibilities of each team member in this new structure.
items.note: A polite way to ask for clarification without implying fault, common in meetings.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that a possibility is still open for consideration, despite reservations.
items.example: I'm not entirely ruling out the option of outsourcing, but we need to explore internal solutions first.
items.plain: I'm not completely dismissing the option of outsourcing, but we need to explore internal solutions first.
items.note: Suggests flexibility and openness to ideas, even if not fully committed yet.

items.meaning: Used to indicate mild agreement or a willingness to consider something, despite initial hesitation.
items.example: I'm not entirely opposed to extending the deadline if it means a higher quality deliverable.
items.plain: I'm not completely against extending the deadline if it means a higher quality deliverable.
items.note: A diplomatic way to express conditional acceptance or a lack of strong objection.

items.meaning: Used to express uncertainty about specific details or the nature of something.
items.example: I'm not entirely sure what the client expects from us regarding the final report format.
items.plain: I don't know exactly what the client expects from us regarding the final report format.
items.note: A common way to admit a lack of precise information, often preceding a question.

items.meaning: Used to express uncertainty about the method or process for achieving something.
items.example: I'm not entirely sure how we can implement this new policy without disrupting current operations.
items.plain: I don't know exactly how we can implement this new policy without disrupting current operations.
items.note: Indicates a need for more planning or clarification on the practical steps.

items.meaning: Used to express uncertainty about the reason or justification for something.
items.example: I'm not entirely sure why the previous team decided to use this outdated software.
items.plain: I don't know exactly why the previous team decided to use this outdated software.
items.note: Often used when questioning past decisions or seeking a deeper understanding of motives.

items.meaning: Used to express uncertainty about a condition or the truth of a statement.
items.example: I'm not entirely sure if the budget allows for such a significant upgrade at this time.
items.plain: I don't know if the budget allows for such a significant upgrade at this time.
items.note: A polite way to express doubt about a possibility or a factual constraint.

items.meaning: Used to suggest a specific course of action or strategy for progress.
items.example: The way forward is to gather more data before making any hasty decisions.
items.plain: The next step is to gather more data before making any hasty decisions.
items.note: Clearly states a proposed next step, often after a period of analysis.

items.meaning: Used to state the essential point or the most important fact of a situation.
items.example: The bottom line is, we need to deliver this project on time and within budget.
items.plain: The most important thing is, we need to deliver this project on time and within budget.
items.note: Emphasizes the ultimate truth or core requirement, often used to cut to the chase.

items.text: The long and short of it is
items.form: The long and short of it is
items.meaning: Used to summarize the main facts of a situation concisely, omitting details.
items.example: The long and short of it is, we missed a critical deadline due to unforeseen technical issues.
items.plain: In summary, we missed a critical deadline due to unforeseen technical issues.
items.note: An informal but common way to quickly get to the main point, often used in explanations.

items.text: The reality of the situation is
items.form: The reality of the situation is
items.meaning: Used to state the true facts of a situation, often contrasting with assumptions or hopes.
items.example: The reality of the situation is, we don't have the resources to take on another major client right now.
items.plain: The truth is, we don't have the resources to take on another major client right now.
items.note: Used to bring a dose of realism to a discussion, often when facing difficult truths.

items.text: The truth of the matter is
items.form: The truth of the matter is
items.meaning: Used to state the actual facts, often to clarify or correct a misunderstanding.
items.example: The truth of the matter is, the budget was approved, but the funds haven't been released yet.
items.plain: Actually, the budget was approved, but the funds haven't been released yet.
items.note: Emphasizes the factual basis of a statement, often used to set the record straight.

items.text: The fact of the matter is
items.form: The fact of the matter is
items.meaning: Used to state the actual facts, often to emphasize a point or correct a misconception.
items.example: The fact of the matter is, our competitors are already implementing similar solutions.
items.plain: Actually, our competitors are already implementing similar solutions.
items.note: Similar to 'the truth of the matter is', used to underscore a factual point.

items.meaning: Used to emphasize the main idea or purpose of what is being said.
items.example: The point is, we need to learn from this mistake and prevent it from happening again.
items.plain: The main idea is, we need to learn from this mistake and prevent it from happening again.
items.note: A direct way to highlight the core message or objective, often used to refocus.

items.meaning: Used to refer to the current problem or topic being discussed.
items.example: The issue at hand is how to reallocate tasks to cover for the absent team member.
items.plain: The current problem is how to reallocate tasks to cover for the absent team member.
items.note: A formal way to specify the immediate subject of discussion or concern.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a key query or the central problem that needs to be addressed.
items.example: The question is, can we realistically meet these aggressive targets without compromising quality?
items.plain: The main problem is, can we realistically meet these aggressive targets without compromising quality?
items.note: Frames the core dilemma or decision point, inviting discussion or a solution.

items.meaning: To collaborate and work together to solve a problem or generate ideas.
items.example: Let's put our heads together after lunch and see if we can find a way forward.
items.plain: Let's collaborate after lunch and see if we can find a way forward.
items.note: An informal but common expression for teamwork and brainstorming.

items.meaning: To discuss ideas with someone to get their feedback and perspective.
items.example: Could I bounce some ideas off you about the project proposal before I finalize it?
items.plain: Could I discuss some ideas with you about the project proposal before I finalize it?
items.note: Suggests an informal, exploratory discussion to refine thoughts.

items.meaning: To do everything possible to find a solution or gather information.
items.example: We need to leave no stone unturned in our investigation to understand the system failure.
items.plain: We need to do everything possible in our investigation to understand the system failure.
items.note: Emphasizes thoroughness and persistence in problem-solving or searching.

items.meaning: To think creatively and unconventionally, beyond traditional methods.
items.example: This complex issue requires us to think outside the box for truly innovative solutions.
items.plain: This complex issue requires us to think creatively for truly innovative solutions.
items.note: Encourages innovative thinking, often used when conventional approaches have failed.

items.meaning: To discreetly ask someone for their opinion or reaction before making a formal proposal.
items.example: I'll sound out the team lead on the new project idea before presenting it to management.
items.plain: I'll discreetly ask the team lead for their opinion on the new project idea before presenting it to management.
items.note: Suggests a preliminary, informal inquiry to gauge reception or gather initial feedback.

items.meaning: To try something out cautiously before committing fully, to see how it goes.
items.example: We should test the waters with a small pilot program before rolling out the new software company-wide.
items.plain: We should try a small pilot program before rolling out the new software company-wide.
items.note: Implies a cautious, experimental approach to gauge reaction or feasibility.

items.meaning: To understand or perceive something, often intuitively or generally.
items.example: I need to talk to the client again to get a sense of their true priorities for this phase.
items.plain: I need to talk to the client again to understand their true priorities for this phase.
items.note: Refers to gaining an overall impression or understanding, not necessarily precise details.

items.meaning: To develop an intuitive understanding or familiarity with something.
items.example: Let's run a small test to get a feel for how the new system performs under pressure.
items.plain: Let's run a small test to understand how the new system performs under pressure.
items.note: Similar to 'get a sense of', often implies hands-on experience or observation.

items.meaning: To understand a situation or a person's intentions or mood.
items.example: I'm trying to get a read on the market's reaction to our competitor's recent product launch.
items.plain: I'm trying to understand the market's reaction to our competitor's recent product launch.
items.note: Informal but common, implies assessing a situation or person's state of mind.

items.meaning: To take control of a situation, often one that is becoming difficult or chaotic.
items.example: We need to get a grip on these escalating costs before they impact our profitability.
items.plain: We need to take control of these escalating costs before they impact our profitability.
items.note: Suggests regaining control or understanding of a challenging situation.

items.meaning: To be essentially a matter of; to be the most important factor.
items.example: Ultimately, the success of this project comes down to effective teamwork and communication.
items.plain: Ultimately, the success of this project depends on effective teamwork and communication.
items.note: Used to simplify a complex situation to its core element or deciding factor.

items.meaning: To face a difficult or unpleasant situation with courage and endure it.
items.example: We'll just have to bite the bullet and work extra hours to meet this tight deadline.
items.plain: We'll just have to face the difficult situation and work extra hours to meet this tight deadline.
items.note: Implies accepting an unavoidable hardship, often with a sense of resignation.

items.meaning: To commit to a course of action after hesitation, especially a significant one.
items.example: After much deliberation, we decided to take the plunge and invest in the new technology.
items.plain: After much deliberation, we decided to commit and invest in the new technology.
items.note: Suggests a bold decision after a period of uncertainty or careful thought.

items.meaning: To consider something carefully and reflect on it.
items.example: I'll give it some thought over the weekend and get back to you with my decision.
items.plain: I'll consider it over the weekend and get back to you with my decision.
items.note: A polite way to indicate that a decision or idea requires careful consideration.

items.meaning: To delay making a decision until the next day, allowing time for reflection.
items.example: This is a big decision, so I'd like to sleep on it before giving you an answer.
items.plain: This is a big decision, so I'd like to wait until tomorrow before giving you an answer.
items.note: An informal but widely accepted way to request time for careful consideration.

items.meaning: To think about something carefully and at length, often before making a decision.
items.example: I need a few days to mull it over before I can offer a comprehensive proposal.
items.plain: I need a few days to think about it carefully before I can offer a comprehensive proposal.
items.note: Suggests a process of deep, unhurried consideration, often for complex issues.

items.meaning: To consider something as a relevant factor when making a decision or judgment.
items.example: We must take into account the potential impact on employee morale when implementing these changes.
items.plain: We must consider the potential impact on employee morale when implementing these changes.
items.note: Emphasizes including all relevant factors in a decision-making process.

items.meaning: To include something as a relevant element or consideration.
items.example: Did you factor in the increased shipping costs when calculating the project budget?
items.plain: Did you include the increased shipping costs when calculating the project budget?
items.note: A concise way to ask if a specific element has been considered in calculations or plans.

items.meaning: To remember a piece of information or a fact, especially when making decisions.
items.example: Please bear in mind that the client has a very tight budget for this particular task.
items.plain: Please remember that the client has a very tight budget for this particular task.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal way to remind someone of an important consideration.

items.meaning: To remember a piece of information or a fact, especially when making decisions.
items.example: We need to keep in mind the long-term sustainability of any solution we propose.
items.plain: We need to remember the long-term sustainability of any solution we propose.
items.note: Similar to 'bear in mind', but slightly less formal and very common.

items.meaning: To be willing to consider new ideas or opinions, even if they differ from one's own.
items.example: Let's keep an open mind during the brainstorming session; all suggestions are welcome.
items.plain: Let's be willing to consider new ideas during the brainstorming session; all suggestions are welcome.
items.note: Encourages receptiveness to diverse perspectives, crucial for effective problem-solving.

items.meaning: To avoid making a final decision too soon, allowing for flexibility and alternative choices.
items.example: For now, let's keep our options open regarding the vendor until we receive all quotes.
items.plain: For now, let's avoid making a final decision regarding the vendor until we receive all quotes.
items.note: Suggests a strategic delay in commitment to maintain flexibility.

items.meaning: To avoid risks and choose the safest or most cautious course of action.
items.example: Given the uncertainties, I think we should play it safe and stick to the proven method.
items.plain: Given the uncertainties, I think we should avoid risks and stick to the proven method.
items.note: Implies a preference for caution and minimal risk, often in uncertain situations.

items.meaning: To decide how to deal with a situation as it develops, rather than planning in advance.
items.example: We don't have all the information yet, so let's play it by ear for the next few days.
items.plain: We don't have all the information yet, so let's decide as the situation develops for the next few days.
items.note: Suggests flexibility and adaptability, often when faced with unpredictable circumstances.

items.meaning: To clarify or explain something, making it easier to understand.
items.example: Could you shed some light on why the project budget was suddenly increased?
items.plain: Could you explain why the project budget was suddenly increased?
items.note: Commonly used when seeking clarification or an explanation for a confusing situation.

items.meaning: A specific issue or detail that causes disagreement or difficulty, preventing progress.
items.example: The allocation of resources has become a sticking point in our negotiations with the partner.
items.plain: The allocation of resources has become a difficult issue in our negotiations with the partner.
items.note: Highlights a particular obstacle that is hard to resolve, often in negotiations.

items.meaning: A point in a process where progress slows down or stops, causing delays.
items.example: The approval process is currently a bottleneck, delaying all subsequent project phases.
items.plain: The approval process is currently causing delays, slowing all subsequent project phases.
items.note: Identifies a specific constraint that impedes efficiency or flow.

items.meaning: To identify the exact nature or location of an issue with precision.
items.example: We need to pinpoint the problem with the software before we can develop a fix.
items.plain: We need to identify the exact problem with the software before we can develop a fix.
items.note: Emphasizes the need for precise identification of the core issue.

items.meaning: To indicate a larger, underlying issue or trend.
items.example: The recent decline in sales is symptomatic of deeper issues within our marketing strategy.
items.plain: The recent decline in sales indicates deeper issues within our marketing strategy.
items.note: Suggests that a visible problem is merely a sign of a more fundamental, hidden issue.

items.meaning: Something that helps cause a particular outcome or problem.
items.example: Lack of clear communication was a contributing factor to the project's delay.
items.plain: Lack of clear communication helped cause the project's delay.
items.note: Identifies one element among several that led to a specific result.

items.meaning: A major obstacle or difficulty that must be overcome.
items.example: Securing adequate funding remains a significant hurdle for the expansion plan.
items.plain: Securing adequate funding remains a major obstacle for the expansion plan.
items.note: Highlights a substantial challenge that requires considerable effort to surmount.

items.meaning: To meet with opposition, unwillingness to cooperate, or difficulty.
items.example: We encountered resistance from some departments regarding the new data privacy regulations.
items.plain: We met opposition from some departments regarding the new data privacy regulations.
items.note: Describes facing opposition or difficulty, often from people or established systems.

items.text: to be a cause for concern
items.meaning: Something that gives reason to worry or be anxious.
items.example: The unexpected drop in server performance is definitely a cause for concern.
items.plain: The unexpected drop in server performance is definitely something to worry about.
items.note: A formal way to state that something is worrying, often used in reports or meetings.

items.meaning: An urgent issue that needs immediate attention or action.
items.example: Resolving the client's complaint is a pressing matter that requires our full focus.
items.plain: Resolving the client's complaint is an urgent issue that requires our full focus.
items.note: Emphasizes the urgency and importance of an issue, demanding prompt resolution.

items.meaning: An important point or factor that must be thought about carefully.
items.example: User experience is always a key consideration when developing new software features.
items.plain: User experience is always an important point when developing new software features.
items.note: Identifies a crucial factor that influences decisions or outcomes.

items.meaning: An obstacle or difficulty that prevents progress or success.
items.example: Lack of clear leadership proved to be a stumbling block for the entire initiative.
items.plain: Lack of clear leadership proved to be an obstacle for the entire initiative.
items.note: Highlights a specific impediment that hinders advancement.

items.meaning: A difficult or complicated circumstance that requires careful handling.
items.example: Dealing with the conflicting demands of two major stakeholders is a tricky situation.
items.plain: Dealing with the conflicting demands of two major stakeholders is a difficult circumstance.
items.note: Describes a complex scenario that needs skill and diplomacy to navigate.

items.meaning: A sensitive issue requiring careful and tactful handling to avoid offense or problems.
items.example: Discussing budget cuts with the team is always a delicate matter that needs careful preparation.
items.plain: Discussing budget cuts with the team is always a sensitive issue that needs careful preparation.
items.note: Implies that an issue is sensitive and requires diplomacy and caution.

items.meaning: A difficult and often controversial problem that is hard to resolve.
items.example: Employee compensation remains a thorny issue that we need to address in the next quarter.
items.plain: Employee compensation remains a difficult and controversial problem that we need to address in the next quarter.
items.note: Describes a problem that is complex, contentious, and potentially painful to deal with.

items.meaning: Something unclear, undefined, or open to interpretation, lacking clear rules.
items.example: The company policy on remote work is still a grey area, causing some confusion.
items.plain: The company policy on remote work is still unclear, causing some confusion.
items.note: Refers to a situation where rules or definitions are ambiguous, leading to uncertainty.

items.meaning: An idea or plan that has no chance of success or is not worth pursuing.
items.example: Proposing a complete overhaul of the system right now would be a non-starter.
items.plain: Proposing a complete overhaul of the system right now would have no chance of success.
items.note: Indicates that an idea is unfeasible or unacceptable from the outset.

items.meaning: A difficult or demanding task or request.
items.example: Completing the entire project by Friday is a tall order, but we'll do our best.
items.plain: Completing the entire project by Friday is a difficult task, but we'll do our best.
items.note: Suggests a challenging request that will require significant effort to fulfill.

items.text: to be a tough nut to crack
items.meaning: A difficult problem or person to deal with or understand.
items.example: This persistent bug in the software is proving to be a tough nut to crack.
items.plain: This persistent bug in the software is proving to be a difficult problem to solve.
items.note: Informal but common, describes something very challenging to resolve or comprehend.

items.meaning: A continuing unpleasant situation that causes itself and is difficult to escape.
items.example: The lack of training leads to errors, which then require more training; it's a vicious circle.
items.plain: The lack of training leads to errors, which then require more training; it's a continuing unpleasant situation.
items.note: Describes a self-perpetuating negative cycle, often hard to break.

items.meaning: Something that has both advantages and disadvantages, or positive and negative effects.
items.example: Expanding rapidly can be a double-edged sword, bringing growth but also increased risks.
items.plain: Expanding rapidly can have both advantages and disadvantages, bringing growth but also increased risks.
items.note: Highlights the dual nature of something, where benefits come with drawbacks.

items.meaning: A course of action that will lead to increasingly bad or undesirable results.
items.example: Compromising on quality standards could be a slippery slope towards losing customer trust.
items.plain: Compromising on quality standards could lead to increasingly bad results towards losing customer trust.
items.note: Warns that a seemingly small negative step could lead to a series of worse outcomes.

items.meaning: An event that makes one realize a problem or danger that was previously ignored.
items.example: The recent security breach was a wake-up call for us to invest more in cybersecurity.
items.plain: The recent security breach made us realize we needed to invest more in cybersecurity.
items.note: Describes an event that forces a realization of a serious issue, prompting action.

items.meaning: Something that significantly alters a situation, strategy, or outcome.
items.example: The new AI integration could be a game changer for our product development process.
items.plain: The new AI integration could significantly alter our product development process.
items.note: Describes an innovation or event that fundamentally changes the competitive landscape.

items.text: to weigh the pros and cons
items.meaning: To consider the advantages and disadvantages of a particular course of action.
items.example: Before deciding, we need to carefully weigh the pros and cons of each proposed solution.
items.plain: Before deciding, we need to carefully consider the advantages and disadvantages of each proposed solution.
items.note: A common and clear way to describe the process of evaluating options.

items.meaning: To reduce the number of available choices or possibilities.
items.example: Let's narrow down the options to the top three most viable solutions for further analysis.
items.plain: Let's reduce the number of options to the top three most viable solutions for further analysis.
items.note: Describes the process of making a selection from a larger set of choices.

items.meaning: To make a decision based on one's own discretion and assessment, often without clear rules.
items.example: Ultimately, it's up to the project manager to make a judgment call on the best approach.
items.plain: Ultimately, it's up to the project manager to make a decision based on their own assessment on the best approach.
items.note: Implies a decision made based on experience and intuition rather than strict guidelines.

items.meaning: To investigate every possible method or approach to solve a problem.
items.example: We must explore all avenues to find a sustainable energy source for the new facility.
items.plain: We must investigate every possible method to find a sustainable energy source for the new facility.
items.note: Emphasizes a comprehensive search for solutions, leaving no possibility unexamined.

items.meaning: To think about the possible future effects or consequences of an action or decision.
items.example: Before launching, we need to carefully consider the implications of this new feature on user privacy.
items.plain: Before launching, we need to carefully think about the possible future effects of this new feature on user privacy.
items.note: Highlights the importance of foresight and understanding potential outcomes.

items.meaning: To plan a detailed course of action to achieve a specific goal.
items.example: Let's map out a strategy for improving customer retention over the next six months.
items.plain: Let's plan a detailed course of action for improving customer retention over the next six months.
items.note: Suggests a thorough and systematic approach to planning.

items.meaning: To create a rough outline or preliminary version of a plan.
items.example: Can you quickly sketch out a plan for the emergency response protocol?
items.plain: Can you quickly create a rough outline of a plan for the emergency response protocol?
items.note: Implies creating a basic, non-detailed plan, often as a starting point.

items.text: to put a proposal on the table
items.form: put a proposal on the table
items.meaning: To formally suggest an idea or plan for consideration and discussion.
items.example: I'd like to put a proposal on the table for restructuring the project teams.
items.plain: I'd like to formally suggest an idea for restructuring the project teams.
items.note: A formal way to introduce an idea for collective review and decision-making.

items.meaning: To understand a situation fully and without confusion.
items.example: We need more data to get a clear picture of the market trends before investing.
items.plain: We need more data to understand the market trends fully before investing.
items.note: Emphasizes the need for comprehensive understanding to make informed decisions.

items.meaning: To improve one's comprehension or knowledge of something.
items.example: Let's review the report again to get a better understanding of the financial projections.
items.plain: Let's review the report again to improve our comprehension of the financial projections.
items.note: Suggests a need for deeper insight or clarification on a topic.

items.meaning: To view a situation from a new or different angle, often by seeking outside input.
items.example: Inviting an external consultant might help us get a fresh perspective on this long-standing problem.
items.plain: Inviting an external consultant might help us view this long-standing problem from a new angle.
items.note: Encourages seeking new viewpoints to overcome entrenched thinking.

items.meaning: To consider a situation from an alternative viewpoint or approach.
items.example: Perhaps we should talk to the sales team to get a different angle on customer feedback.
items.plain: Perhaps we should talk to the sales team to consider customer feedback from an alternative viewpoint.
items.note: Similar to 'fresh perspective', but often implies seeking a specific, alternative viewpoint.

items.text: to get a new take on
items.meaning: To consider a new interpretation or understanding of a situation or idea.
items.example: I'm hoping the workshop will help us get a new take on how to approach client engagement.
items.plain: I'm hoping the workshop will help us consider a new interpretation of how to approach client engagement.
items.note: Suggests gaining a novel or updated understanding of a subject.

to be a key consideration.note: Checker slip: The key definition accurately captures the meaning of an important factor to consider in the given context.
